body.text: In recent months, India’s opposition parties, students, and civil society organizations have participated in a wave of protests against the Narendra Modi government. The protests are unprecedented for several reasons. Large numbers are out on the streets protesting. Opposition political parties appear more united; they have rallied behind the leadership of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi. Importantly, the fear of reprisals for criticizing Prime Minister Modi seems to have loosened its grip on a section of Indian society.

Public intellectual Ashok Swain, who is professor of Peace and Conflict Research at Uppsala University, shared his insights on the nature of this opposition to Modi’s rule with The Diplomat’s South Asia editor Sudha Ramachandran. Drawing attention to the massive youth mobilization in the protests, he pointed out that “a generation previously considered politically passive is willing to confront the government directly.”

Unlike the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the left student organizations are working with the INDIA bloc of opposition parties. “They may disagree with Congress on economic policies or other ideological questions… but they recognize the importance of building a united front against authoritarianism,” he said.

Swain warned against boycotting of elections to pressure the government. “An electoral boycott might undermine the government’s democratic credibility, but it could simultaneously strengthen its practical control over political institutions,” he said.
There is a change in the mood in India, as well as the diaspora, in the way they perceive the Narendra Modi government. Could you throw light on this?

There is certainly a noticeable change in the political mood, both within India and among sections of the Indian diaspora. For more than a decade, Narendra Modi successfully projected himself as an almost invincible leader who alone could provide India with strong governance, economic development, and international prestige. That image is increasingly being questioned. The change has not happened overnight. It is the cumulative result of economic disappointments, growing unemployment, institutional decline, social and religious polarization, and the government’s increasingly authoritarian behavior.

Modi’s political success depended heavily on controlling and manipulating the public narrative. Through a largely compliant mainstream media, aggressive social media campaigns, and the constant use of Hindu nationalism, the BJP managed to divert public attention from failures in governance. Criticism of Modi was routinely portrayed as criticism of India itself. Anyone questioning the government risked being labelled anti-national.

However, propaganda cannot indefinitely conceal people’s everyday experiences. Young Indians face unemployment, competitive examinations have been compromised by repeated paper leaks, economic inequality continues to widen, and ordinary families struggle with rising living costs. The gap between the government’s claims and people’s lived realities has become increasingly difficult to ignore.

The youth protests have been particularly significant. They demonstrate that a generation previously considered politically passive is willing to confront the government directly. The controversy over electoral rolls has added another dimension: people are increasingly questioning not only the government’s performance but also the fairness of the democratic process itself.

The diaspora is also changing, although it would be wrong to suggest that Modi has lost its support entirely. Hindutva organizations outside India remain influential, particularly among affluent and politically organized sections of the diaspora. However, many Indians living abroad are becoming uncomfortable with the contradiction between celebrating democracy in their adopted countries and defending majoritarian authoritarianism in India.

Rahul Gandhi’s growing political standing is another important factor. For years, Modi and the BJP successfully ridiculed him. But Gandhi has remained remarkably consistent in opposing Hindutva and defending India’s constitutional democracy. It is not so much that Gandhi has changed; rather, India is beginning to change, and more people are now willing to listen to what he has been saying.

The important development, in and outside India among Indians, is that fear is gradually being replaced by political confidence. Modi remains in power, but his aura of invincibility has been seriously weakened.

You have written that the CJP, which led the protests at Jantar Mantar in July, “has been pushed from the center of a political confrontation [with the Modi government] it hoped to lead.” Why has this happened?

The Cockroach Janata Party achieved something extraordinary in July. A movement that began with satire on social media managed to mobilize thousands of young Indians and eventually contributed to the resignation of a Union Minister. It demonstrated the political potential of spontaneous youth mobilization at a time when established opposition parties had struggled to challenge the Modi government effectively. However, the very factors that made the CJP successful in July also exposed its limitations when it attempted to repeat that success.

First, the two movements concerned fundamentally different issues. Examination paper leaks and unemployment directly affected millions of young people. The CJP could articulate their anger through a simple and emotionally powerful demand. The campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar involves electoral institutions, constitutional accountability, and the future of democratic competition. Political parties have a much greater organizational and institutional stake in these questions.

Second, the CJP lost the element of surprise. In July, the government underestimated the movement. By October, it understood the potential threat and acted pre-emptively, restricting protest spaces and detaining organizers. The movement’s dependence on a few prominent personalities and a central protest location, Jantar Mantar, became a serious weakness.

Third, the CJP had not developed the organizational infrastructure necessary to sustain a nationwide political confrontation. Social media can mobilize anger, but it cannot substitute for district-level and village-level organizations, experienced leadership, legal support, and political coordination.

There is also a strategic problem. The CJP appeared reluctant to accept that Gandhi and the established opposition had already been challenging electoral irregularities. Instead of building a complementary relationship, it sometimes seemed to compete for leadership of the agitation.

A successful protest does not automatically produce a sustainable movement. The CJP should not interpret cooperation with opposition parties as surrendering its independence. Its greatest contribution could be to remain an independent youth movement while working with broader democratic forces on shared objectives. Its July success showed that it could ignite public anger. Its subsequent difficulties demonstrate that sustaining political resistance requires organization, alliances and strategic smartness.

In contrast to the CJP, the leftist student organizations have shown willingness to work with the Congress-led INDIA bloc of parties against the government. What explains the difference in their approach?

The difference is primarily one of political experience, organizational maturity, and understanding the nature of the struggle against the Modi government. Left student organizations such as the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), the All India Students’ Association (AISA), and the All India Students’ Federation (AISF) have long histories of political mobilization. They understand that student movements cannot remain isolated from larger political developments, particularly when the issues concern democratic rights and constitutional institutions.

These organizations also recognize that the present confrontation is not merely about removing an individual minister or chief election commissioner. It concerns the future of India’s constitutional democracy and the continuing attempt by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh-BJP [the RSS is the ruling BJP’s ideological mentor] to transform India into a Hindu majoritarian state. For them, cooperation with Congress and the INDIA alliance is therefore a strategic necessity rather than an ideological compromise.

The CJP, by contrast, emerged from a spontaneous protest against examination irregularities. Its identity was built partly around rejecting established political parties. That approach helped attract young people disillusioned with conventional politics. But what works for a single-issue protest can become a limitation when the movement confronts a much larger political challenge.

The left student organizations understand another important reality: Rahul Gandhi has emerged as the principal national political figure consistently confronting Modi and Hindutva. They may disagree with Congress on economic policies or other ideological questions, and in a state like Kerala, they are the primary political opponent, but they recognize the importance of building a united front against authoritarianism.

There is a historical lesson here. Authoritarian political projects become stronger when their opponents remain divided over organizational leadership and ideological purity. The CJP needs to understand that independence does not require isolation. It can retain its distinctive identity, mobilize young people and criticize opposition parties when necessary while participating in a broader democratic coalition.
The immediate challenge is not determining which organization receives credit for a protest. It is defending the democratic space within which all these organizations can continue to exist.
What has been the outcome of the INDIA-led rally at Ramlila Maidan on November 1?

The INDIA bloc rally at Ramlila Maidan was politically significant for several reasons. Its importance cannot be measured simply by the number of people attending, although the huge crowd that gathered in Delhi was itself an important political message. What made the rally particularly significant was that the crowd did not consist only of Congress supporters, party workers or members of the INDIA alliance. It also included ordinary citizens without formal political affiliations who had come to express their growing frustration with the Modi government.

That distinction matters enormously. Political parties can mobilize their organizational networks for rallies, but when ordinary people voluntarily participate in large numbers, it suggests that dissatisfaction is moving beyond party politics and developing into a wider public movement. The rally demonstrated that opposition to Modi is increasingly being driven not only by electoral calculations but also by concerns about constitutional democracy, institutional independence and the direction in which the country is heading.

Its second major outcome was the further consolidation of Gandhi’s political leadership. Gandhi is no longer emerging merely as the leader of Congress or even the most prominent figure within the INDIA alliance. He is increasingly becoming the central political figure for parties, organizations and citizens who oppose Modi and his Hindutva brand of politics.

This is an important transformation. For years, Modi’s political strategy relied on portraying Gandhi as weak, inexperienced and incapable of providing national leadership. That strategy is becoming less effective. Gandhi’s consistent opposition to the RSS-BJP’s majoritarian project, his emphasis on constitutional values and his willingness to challenge powerful institutions have dramatically strengthened his credibility.

The rally also demonstrated that the struggle against the government can bring together established political parties, student organizations, civil society activists and ordinary citizens. This is precisely the kind of broad coalition that is necessary to challenge an entrenched authoritarian political project.

However, the rally’s success should not be confused with an electoral victory. Large gatherings create momentum, but that momentum must be translated into sustained organization, opposition unity and effective political mobilization across the country. The Modi government remains in power and retains considerable influence over state institutions and the political narrative. Nevertheless, the rally sent an unmistakable political message: Modi can no longer assume that public discontent will remain fragmented or that Gandhi can be dismissed as a political challenger.
Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following the July protests. However, the Modi government has shown no signs of letting go of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Why?
The difference between Dharmendra Pradhan and Gyanesh Kumar is not simply about their individual importance. It concerns the political consequences their removal would have for the Modi government.

Pradhan is a senior BJP politician, but he is ultimately dispensable. He comes from Odisha, a relatively small state in terms of its weight in national politics, and does not command an independent political base capable of seriously challenging Modi’s leadership. His resignation allowed the government to make a tactical concession without threatening the larger structure of political power. It helped defuse the immediate student agitation and enabled Modi to present the resignation as an act of political responsiveness.

Kumar represents a fundamentally different situation. The demand for his resignation is directly connected to allegations concerning the Election Commission’s conduct, particularly the controversial revision of electoral rolls and questions about the fairness and transparency of elections. These allegations are disputed by the Modi government. Nevertheless, removing Kumar under political pressure would inevitably intensify scrutiny of the Election Commission’s actions in recent years. It would also raise uncomfortable questions about the process through which election commissioners are appointed and the extent of executive influence over an institution constitutionally expected to function independently.

The Modi government would find it much more difficult to contain the political consequences of such a development. There is another, perhaps even more important, consideration. The Modi government’s consolidation of power has depended not only on electoral victories but also on the willingness of a large section of the bureaucracy and constitutional institutions to follow its political direction. If Kumar were sacrificed under pressure, it could send a disturbing signal to officials who have obediently implemented the Modi government’s instructions, including instructions that are considered unlawful or constitutionally questionable.

They might begin to wonder whether loyalty to the political leadership offers any protection when public anger becomes too difficult to manage. For an increasingly centralized government, that uncertainty could have serious consequences. Officials might become more reluctant to implement controversial decisions without adequate legal safeguards.

Therefore, Pradhan’s removal was a manageable political sacrifice. Kumar’s removal could open a much wider debate about institutional independence, electoral legitimacy and bureaucratic accountability. That is why the government has much stronger incentives to protect Kumar, even at the cost of prolonged political confrontation.

There have been calls for the opposition parties to boycott the upcoming assembly elections. What is your view on this? Wouldn’t a boycott of the all-important Uttar Pradesh assembly elections undermine the opposition’s prospects in the general elections?

An electoral boycott is an extremely serious political decision. It should never be treated simply as another form of protest because its consequences could extend far beyond a single election. The opposition’s frustration is understandable. If political parties believe that electoral rolls are being manipulated, constitutional institutions are losing their independence and elections are becoming increasingly unfair, they have legitimate reasons to question the credibility of the electoral process.

A boycott could certainly create a political crisis for the Modi government. If major opposition parties collectively refuse to participate, the government might still conduct elections and claim victory, but the democratic legitimacy of that victory would face serious questions in and outside India. Such a situation could resemble Bangladesh under Sheikh Hasina, where the opposition’s boycott of elections contributed to an increasingly confrontational political environment. The government continued winning elections, but those victories did little to resolve the underlying crisis of political legitimacy.

A similar development in India could seriously damage Modi’s international claim that he leads the world’s largest democracy. However, there is a fundamental problem with this strategy. An electoral boycott might undermine the government’s democratic credibility, but it could simultaneously strengthen its practical control over political institutions.

Without effective electoral competition, the BJP could secure overwhelming legislative majorities, particularly in strategically important states such as Uttar Pradesh. Such victories could provide the government with greater opportunities to advance its Hindutva agenda, including attempts to alter constitutional arrangements and reshape the relationship between the Indian state and its religious minorities.

There is also the question of delimitation, or the redrawing of electoral constituencies. A weakened opposition could find itself unable to resist changes in electoral boundaries and representation that might reshape India’s political balance for decades. Uttar Pradesh is especially important because of its enormous parliamentary representation and central place in national politics. Abandoning electoral competition there could seriously weaken the opposition’s organizational networks, discourage its supporters and damage its prospects in subsequent general elections.

Most importantly, a boycott could contribute to the disappearance of the possibility of a peaceful transfer of power. Democracy survives not simply because elections are held but because those in power can realistically be defeated and replaced through elections. If the opposition withdraws from electoral politics and the government continues ruling without meaningful competition, political conflict may increasingly move from electoral institutions to the streets.

That creates the danger of prolonged confrontation, repression and political instability. Bangladesh’s experience demonstrates how the erosion of credible electoral competition can eventually produce a much deeper crisis of governance. My preference would therefore be for the opposition to continue contesting elections while simultaneously intensifying its political, legal and public campaigns for electoral accountability. It should demand transparent electoral rolls, independent verification, institutional accountability and effective judicial oversight. It should also mobilize citizens to defend their voting rights.

A boycott should remain an absolute last resort, considered only if credible electoral participation becomes impossible and the opposition possesses a united strategy for managing the consequences. The objective must be to defeat authoritarianism while preserving the possibility of democratic change.

India’s opposition must be careful not to surrender the remaining democratic space to a government whose political project, in my assessment, is fundamentally hostile to India’s secular and pluralist constitutional foundations. The greatest danger is not simply that Modi may win another election. It is that India could reach a point where elections no longer provide a credible mechanism for changing the government. Once that happens, the peaceful democratic transition of power that has been central to India’s political system may become impossible.
